transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
The U.K. government says it's investigating
what it calls a serious cyber incident
that forced it to take down nearly all of its online benefits
and pension services.
NPR's Fatima Khasab has more.
A government spokesperson said services were taken down
as a precaution after unusual activity was detected,
and ministers say they're working with the National Cyber Security Centre
and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre
to work out what happened.
The government has not ruled out the possibility that this was a hack,
but say there's currently no evidence that any personal data has been lost
or that a malicious actor has targeted any other government departments.
Officials say regular welfare and pension payments
will be paid as normal, but some Brits have reported
not receiving their benefits as a result of the outage.
Fatima Khasab, NPR News, London.
The U.S. Postal Service is proposing more shipping price hikes
to address its financial challenges.
In Pirasansi Lawang reports,
USPS has already paused certain payments
to retirement funds for postal workers.
Starting January 17th, shipping a package domestically
with the U.S. Postal Service would cost about 6% more on average.
There would also be an 11% surcharge for rising fuel costs.
The Postal Regulatory Commission is now reviewing this proposal.
USPS says it's needed because the self-funded agency
generally receives no tax dollars
and relies on stamp and service fees
to deliver the mail at least six days a week
to just about every address in the country.
Postmaster General David Steiner says
USPS is coming up with new plans to avoid running out of cash in five years.
And I will present those plans to leadership throughout the government
so that they can make the policy choice between reduced levels of service,
a reform of our retirement plans,
and funding the money-losing mandates.
In July, USPS raised the price of a first-class forever stamp to 82 cents.
Hansi Lawang, NPR News.
The first woman and the first black woman
to serve as leader of the New York State Senate has died.
Andrea Stewart-Cousins, who was also an instrumental force
in the state's progressive turn in recent years,
died at her home today at the age of 76.
She served in the state senate for 20 years
and was re-elected this month.
The cause of death hasn't been released.
Today is Black Friday, a day when shoppers hope to get good deals
and many of those shoppers headed to the malls.
Kelly O'Neill was at one in Glendale, California.
I do it over here.
I think the deals maybe haven't been as good recently as they used to be,
but it's still fun to get up and just be out when nobody else is
and see what's out there.
She says she looks forward to in-person shopping on Black Friday.
Meghan Morgan was at a mall in Metteri, Louisiana.
It's lesser, but I mean, we're spending a little bit more
probably sparingly as we used to, but for the most part,
we're just having a good time, and if we see something that catches our eye
and will make us happy, then we're trying to get to the news in the season.
Online shopping is growing, too. This is NPR.
In California, schools in Los Angeles have disabled artificial intelligence
generated summaries in Google searches on school issued devices.
This comes as school districts around the country weigh whether to drop
Google products unless the tech giant allows them to bypass
AI features on school devices.
But Google says AI can't be separated from its search products,
and it warns schools that it will restrict access to search tools
unless those schools allow the use of AI features.
According Kenya has convicted Doomsday cult leader Paul Mackenzie of manslaughter
over the deaths of 123 of his followers.
He's already serving a 200-year sentence for the murder of another 191 people,
almost all of them children in the same mass killing.
Emmanuel Ngunza has more from Nairobi.
The High Court in Mombasa found that Mackenzie persuaded his followers
to fast until they died in Chakaola Forest between 2021 and 2023.
The court found that the plan was for children to die fast,
then women, then men, with Mackenzie himself going last.
Mackenzie said he went to the forest to buy land
and that those who fasted did so on their free will.
Mackenzie's wife was among 29 others convicted while 60 were acquitted.
One of Mackenzie's lawyers says he will appeal this verdict after sentencing.
The deaths came to light in 2023 when hundreds of bodies were found in shallow graves
in one of the worst cult massacres of modern times.
For NPR News, I'm Emmanuel Ngunza in Nairobi.

topics.text: UK government investigating a serious cyber incident that took down nearly all online benefits and pension services
USPS proposes shipping price hikes of about 6% plus an 11% fuel surcharge starting January 17
New York State Senate's first woman and first Black woman leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins dies at 76
Black Friday shoppers visit malls in Glendale, California and Metairie, Louisiana, with mixed views on deals
Los Angeles schools disable AI-generated summaries in Google searches on school-issued devices
Kenyan court convicts Doomsday cult leader Paul Mackenzie of manslaughter over 123 follower deaths
